Chapter 35

Shipping it

The build, the environment, the one adapter setting that ruins your day, and what to check afterwards.

By the end of this chapter

A deployed app that survives a restart, a clock change and a Node upgrade.

Everything green locally. Four things stand between that and a URL somebody can use.

1. The gate

One command. If pnpm run verify is green, the thing is deployable; if it is not, nothing else matters. Put it in CI and make it required.

2. The adapter setting that ruins your day

@sveltejs/adapter-node v6 no longer reads an ORIGIN environment variable at runtime. The trusted origin is baked in at build time from kit.paths.origin, and the header fallback assumes https. Deploy behind a proxy that terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP without the right headers, and every form post returns 403 "Cross-site remote requests are forbidden" — with a perfectly healthy-looking app behind it.

Because it is baked in at build time, PUBLIC_ORIGIN must be correct when you build, not when you start. That catches people whose CI builds an artefact and whose deploy step sets the environment.

3. Dependencies versus devDependencies

Vite bundles devDependencies into the server build. @libsql/client loads a native binary at runtime and cannot be bundled.

Both are needed. Get it wrong and the app builds, deploys, starts, and dies on the first request with Cannot find module '@libsql/linux-x64-gnu'.

4. Pin the runtime

This app depends on the runtime's time zone database and on Intl, so "whatever Node the host feels like" is a real risk. Pinning also makes the ICU-version problem from chapter 32 a decision you make rather than one that happens to you.

Migrations on deploy

Migrations run before the server starts, and they run from the checked-in SQL — never from drizzle-kit push, which compares your schema file to the live database and decides what to do about the difference. That is a fine command for your laptop and a terrible one to point at production.

What to check once it is up

  1. View source on the booking page. The studio name and services should be in the HTML. If you see "Loading…", a pending snippet has escaped onto a page-level boundary.
  2. Book something. Then book the same slot from a second browser and confirm the refusal is polite.
  3. Check the diary updates live in a window you have left open.
  4. Set your phone to another time zone and load the booking page. The times should move; the studio's zone should be named.
  5. Restart the process. Everything should still be there — and PRAGMA journal_mode should still say wal.

What you built

A booking platform that tells the truth about time, cannot double-book, updates itself, works without JavaScript, and is tested well enough that you would deploy it on a Friday.

The three ideas worth carrying to the next thing you build, none of which are about SvelteKit:

  1. Know which layer is the guarantee. Halfpast has three defences against double-booking and exactly one of them is load-bearing. Being able to say which is the difference between a system you trust and one you hope about.
  2. Make the invisible testable. now is an argument, the availability engine is pure, and both daylight-saving transitions run in a fifth of a second. Nothing else about this project would have been provable otherwise.
  3. A client-side check is a courtesy; a server-side check is a control. Build both, and write the test that removes the courtesy.

Checkpoint

pnpm run verify is green, the app is deployed, and all five post-deploy checks pass.
